vignette:
Priya Sharma is a 32-year-old South Asian woman who works as a school counselor at a mid-sized public elementary school in the suburbs of Minneapolis. She is married, college-educated, and until approximately eighteen months ago was regarded by colleagues and family alike as someone of unusual steadiness and warmth. She is now presenting for psychological assessment at the insistence of her husband, who has watched her withdraw from nearly every aspect of the life they built together.

Two years ago, Priya traveled to her mother's home country of Sri Lanka to visit extended family and to volunteer for two weeks with an educational nonprofit working in a region that had experienced intermittent civil unrest. On her third day in a rural district, the convoy of vehicles she was traveling in was caught in the middle of a sudden escalation of violence between armed factions. The vehicles stopped on an exposed road. There was gunfire. Priya was crouched in the back of a minivan alongside four other volunteers and a local translator named Amara, a young woman in her mid-twenties. When the shooting intensified, Priya froze. She did not move toward Amara, who was nearest the door and visibly panicking. Amara opened the door and was struck by debris from an explosion in the seconds that followed. She survived but sustained serious injuries. Priya was physically unharmed. The convoy eventually reached safety, and Priya was evacuated from the country within forty-eight hours.

In the weeks that followed her return to Minneapolis, Priya found herself replaying the moment she froze - not as a coherent recollection but as something that broke through without warning, vivid and disorienting, arriving without context or clear beginning. The memories carried a quality of immediacy that she struggled to articulate, as though time had collapsed and she was still on that road. She began to notice that the sound of a bus engine idling outside her school building, or the hydraulic hiss of its doors, would bring on a sudden, overwhelming return of that feeling - the cramped interior of the van, the noise, the stillness in her own body. She stopped taking the city bus she had relied on for years and began driving to work, adding forty minutes to her commute each way rather than step onto public transit.

What had settled most heavily into Priya's inner life was not the fear itself but the meaning she had made of what she did and did not do. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that she had failed Amara in a way that revealed something essential and damning about her character. She was certain she was weak - not situationally overwhelmed, but fundamentally, constitutionally incapable of rising to a moment that mattered. This belief had migrated into her professional identity in ways that were now affecting her work. As a school counselor, Priya had always been the person students came to in crisis - the adult in the room who stayed calm and knew what to do. She no longer trusted herself to be that person. She had begun deflecting the more acute cases to her supervisor, citing administrative reasons, quietly certain that she was no longer capable of the very thing that had defined her vocation.

She had also, gradually, changed how she appeared in the world. She now wore long sleeves and high necklines regardless of the season, preferring to move through public spaces as inconspicuously as possible. She avoided the television in the evenings, and when her husband watched the news she would leave the room, unwilling to encounter footage of conflict zones or civil unrest that might press against the edges of what she carried. The news had come to feel like an exposure she could not afford.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment at school three weeks ago. A nine-year-old boy came to her office after witnessing a fight on the playground and was visibly shaken. She sat across from him and found she had nothing to offer - her mind went blank, her hands trembled, and she ended the session early. She drove home and told her husband she thought something was seriously wrong. What she fears most, sitting in the intake room, is that the counselor she used to be is simply gone. What she hopes, though she can barely say it aloud, is that someone will tell her she is not the person she has decided she is.
